concerns.text: FR-005 mandates 't-tests on feature coefficients' for Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models. These are non-parametric, non-linear ensemble methods that do not produce closed-form coefficients or standard errors required for t-tests. Applying t-tests here is a category error; the spec conflates linear model inference with black-box model evaluation.

SC-003 validates the model by measuring 'statistically significant predictors' against a null hypothesis. Since FR-005 applies invalid t-tests to tree-based models (which lack coefficients), the resulting p-values are mathematically undefined or arbitrary. This creates a circular/invalid validation where the 'significance' is an artifact of a misapplied statistical test, not an empirical finding.

The spec proposes using Bonferroni correction on t-tests for feature importance in tree-based models. In materials science fatigue modeling, feature importance in RF/GB is typically derived via permutation or Gini impurity, not coefficient significance. The chosen statistical method (t-test + Bonferroni) is unsuited for the data structure (non-linear, non-additive) of the selected models.

The assumption that 'The relationship between material composition/loading and degradation is primarily linear or non-linear but monotonic' is scientifically weak for fatigue. Fatigue damage often involves threshold effects, interaction terms (e.g., stress ratio x frequency), and non-monotonic regimes (e.g., fatigue limit). Assuming monotonicity may force the model to miss critical failure modes, invalidating the 'composition + loading' hypothesis test.
